claim: High-throughput genomics of SARS-CoV-2 is essential to characterize virus evolution and to identify adaptations that affect pathogenicity or transmission.
source: High-throughput genomics of SARS-CoV-2 is essential to characterize virus evolution and to identify adaptations that affect pathogenicity or transmission.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of genomics for SARS-CoV-2 research, drawing on established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) are commonly considered as driving virus adaption.
source: While single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) are commonly considered as driving virus adaption, RNA recombination events that delete or insert nucleic acid sequences are also critical.
evidence: This reflects established scientific consensus about the role of SNVs in viral evolution.

claim: RNA recombination events that delete or insert nucleic acid sequences are critical for virus adaptation.
source: While single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) are commonly considered as driving virus adaption, RNA recombination events that delete or insert nucleic acid sequences are also critical.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in virology and is a key premise of the study.

claim: Whole genome targeting sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 is typically achieved using pairs of primers to generate cDNA amplicons suitable for next-generation sequencing (NGS).
source: Whole genome targeting sequencing of SARS-CoV-2 is typically achieved using pairs of primers to generate cDNA amplicons suitable for next-generation sequencing (NGS).
evidence: This describes the standard methodology in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: Paired-primer approaches impose constraints on where primers can be designed.
source: However, paired-primer approaches impose constraints on where primers can be designed, how many amplicons are synthesized and requires multiple PCR reactions with non-overlapping primer pools.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the technical requirements of paired-primer methods.

claim: Paired-primer approaches require multiple PCR reactions with non-overlapping primer pools.
source: However, paired-primer approaches impose constraints on where primers can be designed, how many amplicons are synthesized and requires multiple PCR reactions with non-overlapping primer pools.
evidence: This describes a technical limitation of paired-primer methods, based on established knowledge.

claim: Paired-primer approaches impart sensitivity to underlying SNVs.
source: This imparts sensitivity to underlying SNVs and fails to resolve RNA recombination junctions that are not flanked by primer pairs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the technical limitations of paired-primer methods.

claim: Paired-primer approaches fail to resolve RNA recombination junctions that are not flanked by primer pairs.
source: This imparts sensitivity to underlying SNVs and fails to resolve RNA recombination junctions that are not flanked by primer pairs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of paired-primer methods.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq uses hundreds of tiled-primers spaced evenly along the virus genome in a single reverse-transcription reaction.
source: To address these limitations, we have designed an approach called 'Tiled-ClickSeq', which uses hundreds of tiled-primers spaced evenly along the virus genome in a single reverse-transcription reaction.
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in this study.

claim: In Tiled-ClickSeq, the other end of the cDNA amplicon is generated by azido-nucleotides that stochastically terminate cDNA synthesis.
source: The other end of the cDNA amplicon is generated by azido-nucleotides that stochastically terminate cDNA synthesis, removing the need for a paired-primer.
evidence: This describes the technical mechanism of the Tiled-ClickSeq method.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq removes the need for a paired-primer.
source: The other end of the cDNA amplicon is generated by azido-nucleotides that stochastically terminate cDNA synthesis, removing the need for a paired-primer.
evidence: This is a direct consequence of the method design.

claim: A sequencing adaptor containing a Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI) is appended to the cDNA fragment using click-chemistry.
source: A sequencing adaptor containing a Unique Molecular Identifier (UMI) is appended to the cDNA fragment using click-chemistry and a PCR reaction generates a final NGS library.
evidence: This describes a technical step in the Tiled-ClickSeq protocol.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq provides complete genome coverage, including the 5'UTR, at high depth and specificity to the virus on both Illumina and Nanopore NGS platforms.
source: Tiled-ClickSeq provides complete genome coverage, including the 5'UTR, at high depth and specificity to the virus on both Illumina and Nanopore NGS platforms.
evidence: This is a claim about the performance of the method that is supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq can simultaneously characterize minority variants, sub-genomic mRNAs (sgmRNAs), structural variants (SVs) and D-RNAs in SARS-CoV-2 isolates and clinical samples.
source: Here, we analyze multiple SARS-CoV-2 isolates and clinical samples to simultaneously characterize minority variants, sub-genomic mRNAs (sgmRNAs), structural variants (SVs) and D-RNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Virus genomics and next-generation sequencing (NGS) are essential components of viral outbreak responses.
source: Virus genomics and next-generation sequencing (NGS) are essential components of viral outbreak responses (Grubaugh et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Reconstruction of consensus genetic sequences is essential to identify adaptations correlated with changes in pathogenicity or transmission.
source: Reconstruction of consensus genetic sequences is essential to identify adaptations correlated with changes in pathogenicity or transmission (Gussow et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Studies of SARS-CoV-2 have identified numerous genomic structural variants (SVs) that arise due to non-homologous RNA recombination.
source: In addition to single nucleotide variations, studies of SARS-CoV-2 have identified numerous genomic structural variants (SVs) (Yi, 2020) that arise due to non-homologous RNA recombination.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: SVs typically comprise small insertions/deletions that nonetheless allow the variant genome to independently replicate and transmit.
source: SVs typically comprise small insertions/deletions that nonetheless allow the variant genome to independently replicate and transmit.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about structural variants in viruses.

claim: Numerous SVs have been described for CoVs including deletions of the accessory open-reading frames (aORFs).
source: Numerous SVs have been described for CoVs including deletions of the accessory open-reading frames (aORFs) (Yc et al., 2020; Muth et al., 2018) and changes in spike protein observed in the B.1.1.7 (Alpha) and other variants of concern (Kemp et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Changes in spike protein have been observed in the B.1.1.7 (Alpha) and other variants of concern.
source: Numerous SVs have been described for CoVs including deletions of the accessory open-reading frames (aORFs) (Yc et al., 2020; Muth et al., 2018) and changes in spike protein observed in the B.1.1.7 (Alpha) and other variants of concern (Kemp et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Small deletions arise near the furin cleavage site of spike protein during amplification of SARS-CoV-2 on Vero cells.
source: Adaptation of SARS-CoV-2 also occurs during passaging in cell-culture, such as small deletions that arise near the furin cleavage site of spike protein during amplification on Vero cells (Ogando et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Deletions near the furin cleavage site can alter the fitness and virulence of SARS-CoV-2 isolates.
source: These deletions can alter the fitness and virulence of SARS-CoV-2 isolates and thus must be genetically characterized at the within-culture population level prior to passaged stock use in subsequent studies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological significance of the furin cleavage site and cited work.

claim: Non-homologous RNA recombination gives rise to defective-RNAs (D-RNAs), also known as defective viral genomes (DVGs).
source: Similar to SVs, non-homologous RNA recombination also gives rise to defective-RNAs (D-RNAs), also known as defective viral denomes (DVGs).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in virology.

claim: D-RNAs have been observed in multiple studies of coronaviruses (CoVs), including mouse hepatitis virus (MHV).
source: D-RNAs have been observed in multiple studies of coronaviruses (CoVs), including mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) (Makino et al., 1984; Makino et al., 1985; Makino et al., 1988a; Makino et al., 1988b), bovine CoV (Chang et al., 1994), avian infectious bronchitis virus (IBV) (Penzes et al., 1995), human CoV 299E (Viehweger et al., 2019; Banerjee et al., 2001; Joo et al., 1996; Kim et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 is >10-fold more recombinogenic in cell culture than other CoVs such as MERS.
source: We recently demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 is >10-fold more recombinogenic in cell culture than other CoVs such as MERS (Gribble et al., 2021) and generates abundant D-RNAs containing RNA recombination junctions that most commonly flank U-rich RNA sequences.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 generates abundant D-RNAs containing RNA recombination junctions that most commonly flank U-rich RNA sequences.
source: We recently demonstrated that SARS-CoV-2 is >10-fold more recombinogenic in cell culture than other CoVs such as MERS (Gribble et al., 2021) and generates abundant D-RNAs containing RNA recombination junctions that most commonly flank U-rich RNA sequences.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: D-RNAs may change the fitness, disease outcomes, and vaccine effectiveness for SARS-CoV-2 similar to other respiratory pathogens such as influenza and RSV.
source: D-RNAs may change the fitness, disease outcomes, and vaccine effectiveness for SARS-CoV-2 similar to other respiratory pathogens such as influenza and RSV (Vignuzzi and Lopez, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on analogy to other viruses, supported by a citation.

claim: The ARTIC approach can reliably identify SNVs and minority variants present in as little as 3% of genomes.
source: Perhaps the most popular method for SARS-CoV-2 sequencing is the 'ARTIC' approach (Tyson et al., 2020), which can reliably identify SNVs and minority variants present in as little as 3% of genomes (Grubaugh et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work describing the ARTIC method.

claim: The requirement for pairs of primers constrains where amplicons can be designed and imparts sensitivity to single nucleotide variants (SNVs).
source: However, the requirement for pairs of primers constrains where amplicons can be designed and imparts sensitivity to single nucleotide variants (SNVs).
evidence: This is an inference about the technical limitations of paired-primer methods.

claim: Multiple PCR reactions containing different pools of paired-primers must be performed in order to obtain cDNA amplicons of the correct size and to prevent the interaction or mis-priming of PCR primers.
source: Multiple PCR reactions containing different pools of paired-primers must also be performed in order to obtain cDNA amplicons of the correct size and to prevent the interaction or mis-priming of PCR primers.
evidence: This describes a technical requirement of paired-primer methods based on established knowledge.

claim: Pairs of primers that do not flank RNA recombination junctions will be unable to detect unexpected or unpredicted RNA recombinant species.
source: Importantly, pairs of primers that do not flank RNA recombination junctions will be unable to detect unexpected or unpredicted RNA recombinant species.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of paired-primer approaches.

claim: Paired-primer approaches necessitate the re-design and validation of alternative sets of primer-pairs for each specific NGS platform used.
source: Finally, paired-primer approaches also necessitate the re-design and validation of alternative sets of primer-pairs for each specific NGS platform used (e.g. Illumina amplicons are 200–500 nts, Nanopore amplicons are ~2000–5000 nts).
evidence: This describes a practical limitation of paired-primer methods based on platform requirements.

claim: ClickSeq is a click-chemistry-based platform for NGS that prevents artifactual sequence chimeras in the output data.
source: ClickSeq (Routh et al., 2015b; Jaworski and Routh, 2018) is a click-chemistry-based platform for NGS that prevents artifactual sequence chimeras in the output data (Gorzer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work describing the ClickSeq method.

claim: In ClickSeq, the 3'end of an amplified cDNA segment is generated by the stochastic incorporation of terminating 3' azido-nucleotides (AzNTPs) during reverse transcription.
source: Using ClickSeq, the 3'end of an amplified cDNA segment is generated by the stochastic incorporation of terminating 3' azido-nucleotides (AzNTPs) during reverse transcription.
evidence: This describes the technical mechanism of ClickSeq.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq only requires one template-specific primer per cDNA amplicon.
source: Therefore, 'Tiled-ClickSeq' only requires one template-specific primer per cDNA amplicon.
evidence: This is a direct consequence of the method design.

claim: Only one pool of RT-primers is required in Tiled-ClickSeq, even when > 300 template-specific primers and their corresponding cDNA amplicons are generated in the same reaction.
source: Only one pool of RT-primers is required, even when > 300 template-specific primers and their corresponding cDNA amplicons are generated in the same reaction.
evidence: This describes a key feature of the Tiled-ClickSeq method demonstrated in the study.

claim: The same primer set can be used for both Illumina and Nanopore platforms in Tiled-ClickSeq even when requiring different cDNA amplicon sizes.
source: Furthermore, the same primer set can be used for both Illumina and Nanopore platforms even when requiring different cDNA amplicon sizes.
evidence: This is a claim about the versatility of the method that is demonstrated in the study.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq accurately reconstructs full-length viral genomes from multiple isolates of SARS-CoV-2 from both cell-culture and clinical specimens.
source: Here, we utilize the Tiled-ClickSeq method to analyze multiple isolates of SARS-CoV-2 both from cell-culture and clinical specimens used in routine diagnostics for COVID19 and demonstrate that 'Tiled-ClickSeq' accurately reconstructs full-length viral genomes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq captures recombinant RNA species including sgmRNAs, SVs, and D-RNAs.
source: The method also captures recombinant RNA species including sgmRNAs, SVs, and D-RNAs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq libraries can be made from as little as 8 ng of total cellular RNA with only 18 PCR cycles.
source: With this approach, we found that we could robustly make NGS libraries from as little as 8 ng of total cellular RNA with only 18 PCR cycles (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq obtained genome coverage >25 X from nucleotide 3–29823 (50nts from the 3' end of the genome) for the WA-1 strain.
source: Overall, we obtained genome coverage >25 X from nucleotide 3–29823 (50nts from the 3' end of the genome).
evidence: This is a specific result from sequencing the WA-1 strain.

claim: The consensus genome sequence obtained from Tiled-ClickSeq for the WA-1 strain was identical to that already deposited (MT020881) for this isolate.
source: This depth is sufficient to reconstruct a consensus genome sequence that was found to be identical to that already deposited (MT020881) for this isolate (Harcourt et al., 2020a).
evidence: This validates the accuracy of the method by comparison to a reference sequence.

claim: Read coverage from each primer in Tiled-ClickSeq spans approximately 500–600 nts and extends 5'-wards from the tiled RT-primer.
source: The coverage for each primer (denoted by individual colours in Figure 2B) spans approximately 500–600 nts and extends 5'-wards from the tiled RT-primer.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Read coverage from each primer overlaps the read coverage of the upstream primer in Tiled-ClickSeq.
source: Read coverage from each primer overlaps the read coverage of the upstream primer.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the sequencing data.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq allows for continuous gap-free read coverage over the viral genome.
source: This allows for continuous gap-free read coverage over the viral genome which, importantly, allows a downstream cDNA amplicon to provide sequence information over and beyond an upstream primer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overlapping coverage pattern observed.

claim: In Tiled-ClickSeq, each isolate had an average coverage between 4500 and 7500 reads and a coverage of 25 reads in greater than 99.5% (29753/29903 nts) of the SARS-CoV-2 genome for 12 WRCEVA isolates.
source: In the Tiled-ClickSeq data, after UMI deduplication, each isolate had an average coverage between 4500 and 7500 reads and a coverage of 25 reads in greater than 99.5% (29753/29903 nts) of the SARS-CoV-2 genome.
evidence: This is a specific result from the sequencing of 12 WRCEVA isolates.

claim: Read coverage was obtained covering the 5'UTR of each strain ( > 25 reads for all isolates from nucleotide three onwards).
source: Read coverage was also obtained covering the 5'UTR of each strain ( > 25 reads for all isolates from nucleotide three onwards (Figure 3A and B)).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 3A and B.

claim: When using paired-primer approaches, the 5'UTR is ordinarily obscured by the 5'-most primer used in each pool (nts 30–54 for the ARTIC primer set).
source: When using paired-primer approaches, the 5'UTR is ordinarily obscured by the 5'-most primer used in each pool (nts 30–54 for the ARTIC primer set depicted in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a comparison to existing methods, based on knowledge of the ARTIC protocol.

claim: 5–12 SNVs per viral genome were found across the 12 WRCEVA isolates.
source: We found 5–12 SNVs per viral genome (Source data 3), including the prevalent D614G (A23403G) spike adaptation, which enhances SARS-CoV-2 transmission (Plante et al., 2020), in 11 out of the 12 isolates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis of the 12 isolates.

claim: The D614G (A23403G) spike adaptation enhances SARS-CoV-2 transmission.
source: We found 5–12 SNVs per viral genome (Source data 3), including the prevalent D614G (A23403G) spike adaptation, which enhances SARS-CoV-2 transmission (Plante et al., 2020), in 11 out of the 12 isolates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The D614G (A23403G) spike adaptation was found in 11 out of the 12 WRCEVA isolates.
source: We found 5–12 SNVs per viral genome (Source data 3), including the prevalent D614G (A23403G) spike adaptation, which enhances SARS-CoV-2 transmission (Plante et al., 2020), in 11 out of the 12 isolates (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis.

claim: Genome reconstruction using random-primed ClickSeq data yielded identical genomes to the Tiled data for 11 out of 12 isolates.
source: Genome reconstruction was similarly performed using the random-primed ClickSeq data reads. Identical genomes to the Tiled data were obtained for 11 out of 12 isolates, with only one SNV difference in one sample (WRCEVA _000510: T168C).
evidence: This validates the Tiled-ClickSeq method by comparison to random-primed ClickSeq.

claim: Phylogenetic tree reconstruction placed 10 of the WRCEVA isolates in the A2a clade.
source: Phylogenetic tree reconstruction using NextStrain (Hadfield et al., 2018) placed 10 of the isolates in the A2a clade (Figure 3D) and two isolates (WRCEVA_00508, WRCEVA_00513) were Clade B/B1.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis of the sequenced genomes.

claim: Two WRCEVA isolates (WRCEVA_00508, WRCEVA_00513) were Clade B/B1.
source: Phylogenetic tree reconstruction using NextStrain (Hadfield et al., 2018) placed 10 of the isolates in the A2a clade (Figure 3D) and two isolates (WRCEVA_00508, WRCEVA_00513) were Clade B/B1.
evidence: This is a result from phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Reference genomes reconstructed from nanopore data were identical to those generated from the Tiled-ClickSeq Illumina data, with the exception of WRCEVA_000514 which contained a single additional SNV (C14220T).
source: With the exception of WRCEVA_000514 which contained a single additional SNV (C14220T), the reference genomes reconstructed from the nanopore data were identical to those generated from the Tiled-ClickSeq Illumina data.
evidence: This validates the method across different sequencing platforms.

claim: The SNVs reported by the ARTIC protocol were identical to those reported by Tiled-ClickSeq for the same samples.
source: To further validate our approaches, we used the well described ARTIC v3 protocol for amplicon sequencing of whole SARS-CoV-2 viral genomes (Tyson et al., 2020) using the same input RNA as above for Tiled-ClickSeq NGS library synthesis. In every case, the reported SNVs were identical between the ARTIC data and the Tiled-ClickSeq data.
evidence: This validates the accuracy of Tiled-ClickSeq by comparison to an established method.

claim: Across 10 WRCEVA isolates, only 26 minority variants present at >2% were found, all of which were unique within this dataset.
source: Across 10 WRCEVA isolates we found only 26 minority variants present at >2% all of which were unique within this dataset.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the minority variant analysis.

claim: Six WRCEVA isolates reported no minority variants at all.
source: Six isolates reported no minority variants at all.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the minority variant analysis.

claim: All the expected sgmRNAs previously annotated for SARS-CoV-2 were found using Tiled-ClickSeq.
source: We found all the expected sgmRNAs previously annotated for SARS-CoV-2 (Kim et al., 2020) as well as non-canonical sgmRNAs.
evidence: This is a finding from the recombination analysis, validated by comparison to known sgmRNAs.

claim: Non-canonical sgmRNAs were found in SARS-CoV-2 samples using Tiled-ClickSeq.
source: We found all the expected sgmRNAs previously annotated for SARS-CoV-2 (Kim et al., 2020) as well as non-canonical sgmRNAs.
evidence: This is a finding from the recombination analysis.

claim: sgmRNAs were highly enriched in the cellular fractions from expressed icSARS-CoV-2 isolates (comprising >95% of the total viral genetic materials).
source: We found that sgmRNAs were highly enriched in the cellular fractions from expressed icSARS-CoV-2 isolates (comprising >95% of the total viral genetic materials) but were relatively depleted in the supernatant fraction.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis of icSARS-CoV-2 samples.

claim: sgmRNAs were relatively depleted in the supernatant fraction of icSARS-CoV-2 samples.
source: We found that sgmRNAs were highly enriched in the cellular fractions from expressed icSARS-CoV-2 isolates (comprising >95% of the total viral genetic materials) but were relatively depleted in the supernatant fraction.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis.

claim: The depletion of sgmRNAs in the supernatant reflects a strong restriction of the packaging of these RNA species into virions.
source: This reflects a strong restriction of the packaging of these RNA species into virions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed distribution of sgmRNAs.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq and ViReMa accurately reported the expected deletion (Δ23603^23616) in icSARS-CoV-2 samples.
source: In the icSARS-CoV-2 samples, Tiled-ClickSeq and ViReMa accurately reported the expected deletion (Δ23603^23616).
evidence: This validates the method's ability to detect known structural variants.

claim: Small structural variants (Δ23583^23599) were identified in seven of the WRCEVA isolates with a frequency of 2–50%.
source: Interestingly, we also identified small structural variants (Δ23583^23599) in seven of the WRCEVA isolates with a frequency of 2–50%, similar to reports of the selection of variants containing deletions at this site after in vitro passaging on Vero cells (Klimstra et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the structural variant analysis.

claim: A novel SV in one isolate (WRCEVA_000504: Δ27619^27642) was present in 3.5% of the reads resulting in an eight amino acid deletion in ORF7a.
source: We also found a novel SV in one isolate (WRCEVA_000504: Δ27619^27642) present in 3.5% of the reads resulting in an eight amino acid deletion in ORF7a.
evidence: This is a specific finding of a novel structural variant.

claim: From 60 clinical specimens, 36 consensus genomes with greater than 10 x coverage across >99.5% of the viral genome were obtained.
source: From 60 specimens, we obtained 36 consensus genomes with greater than 10 x coverage across >99.5% of the viral genome.
evidence: This is a specific result from the analysis of clinical samples.

claim: At low CT values < 20, all but one clinical sample returned complete genome coverage.
source: At low CT values < 20, all but one sample returned complete genome coverage.
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between CT value and sequencing success.

claim: Between CT values of 20 and 25, genome coverage began to drop with only one complete genome being obtained with a CT >30.
source: Between CTs values of 20 and 25, coverage began to drop with the only one complete genome being obtained with a CT >30.
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between CT value and sequencing success.

claim: Seven out of eight B.1.1.7 lineage isolates with sufficient coverage had a U-to-C transition at the second nucleotide of the genome (U2C).
source: From the 36 reconstructed genomes, 8 were from the B.1.1.7 lineage (Source data 3). Although read coverage is generally diminished at the 5' ends, 7 of these had sufficient coverage ( > 10 x coverage) to assign a U-to-C transition at the second nucleotide of the genome (U2C) (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis of B.1.1.7 variants.

claim: Only 176 genomes in GISAID (out of 2,867,767 genomes on 19th August 2021) contained the U2C SNV.
source: To determine whether this was a novel SNV, we queried all SARS-CoV-2 genomes deposited in the GISAID database (2'867'767 genomes on the 19th August 2021) and extracted the first 30 nts of each genome. Only 176 genomes contained the U2C SNV; 70 of these were from B.1.1.7 'Alpha' VOC and 43 were from the B.1.617.2 'Delta' VOC.
evidence: This is a finding from querying the GISAID database.

claim: 70 genomes with the U2C SNV in GISAID were from B.1.1.7 'Alpha' VOC.
source: Only 176 genomes contained the U2C SNV; 70 of these were from B.1.1.7 'Alpha' VOC and 43 were from the B.1.617.2 'Delta' VOC.
evidence: This is a finding from querying the GISAID database.

claim: 43 genomes with the U2C SNV in GISAID were from the B.1.617.2 'Delta' VOC.
source: Only 176 genomes contained the U2C SNV; 70 of these were from B.1.1.7 'Alpha' VOC and 43 were from the B.1.617.2 'Delta' VOC.
evidence: This is a finding from querying the GISAID database.

claim: An enrichment of small recombination events near the 3'UTR of SARS-CoV-2 was observed in clinical samples.
source: Similar to the distribution of RNA recombination frequencies observed for the cell-culture isolates (both here and in our previous studies [Gribble et al., 2021]), we observe an enrichment of small recombination events near the 3'UTR of SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This is a finding from the recombination analysis of clinical samples.

claim: Two common recombination events (29173^27,802 and 29442^29323) were found in 14 and 17 of the clinical samples respectively at frequencies ranging up to approximately 8%.
source: The two common recombination events in this region that correspond to small duplications (29173^27,802 and 29442^29323, using WA-1 coordinates, indicated Figure 7) were found in 14 and 17 of the clinical samples respectively (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) at frequencies ranging up to approximately 8% of the sequencing reads mapping in these regions.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the recombination analysis.

claim: The common recombination events (29173^27,802 and 29442^29323) found in clinical isolates were not found in any of the cell-culture derived samples.
source: Interestingly, although it is a conserved feature in clinical isolates, it is not found in any of the cell-culture derived samples assayed (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between clinical and cell-culture samples.

claim: Only one clinical sample (MicroGNL-163: B.1.2) had evidence of InDels at the furin cleavage site of Spike protein with 83 unique reads mapping over a 23583^23,599 deletion, corresponding to an approximate frequency of 5%.
source: Interestingly, only one sample (MicroGNL-163: B.1.2) had any evidence of InDels at the furin cleavage site of Spike protein with 83 unique reads mapping over a 23583^23,599 deletion, corresponding to an approximate frequency of 5% of the total virus reads mapping across this locus.
evidence: This is a specific finding about the absence of furin cleavage site deletions in most clinical samples.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq provides a simple method for whole genome sequencing of virus isolates such as SARS-CoV-2 that can simultaneously map SNVs, minority variants as well as recombination events.
source: Tiled-ClickSeq provides a simple method for whole genome sequencing of virus isolates such as SARS-CoV-2 that can simultaneously map SNVs, minority variants as well as recombination events.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Having only a single template-targeted primer per amplicon provides the opportunity to sequence any RNA template regardless of what expected or unknown sequence is found upstream, including recombinant RNA molecules such as sgmRNAs and D-RNAs.
source: Importantly, having only a single template-targeted primer per amplicon provides the opportunity to sequence any RNA template regardless of what expected or unknown sequence is found upstream, including recombinant RNA molecules such as sgmRNAs and D-RNAs.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the method design.

claim: The targeted approach of Tiled-ClickSeq requires a relatively small number of reads to be collected, allowing 10s of samples to be processed on a MiSeq platform or potentially 100s on a single flowcell of a NextSeq.
source: The targeted approach requires a relatively small number of reads to be collected, allowing 10 s of samples to be processed on a MiSeq platform or potentially 100 s on a single flowcell of a NextSeq.
evidence: This is an inference about the scalability of the method based on its efficiency.

claim: The same Tiled-ClickSeq library preps can be used as input in Oxford Nanopore Sequencing pipelines to yield longer reads.
source: Furthermore, the same library preps can be used as input in Oxford Nanopore Sequencing pipelines to yield longer reads, providing the convenience and portability inherent to the platform.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the study.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq can reconstruct full-length SARS-CoV-2 genomes in a manner equivalent to random-primed methods.
source: We demonstrated that this method can reconstruct full-length SARS-CoV-2 genomes in a manner equivalent to random-primed methods.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analysis in the study.

claim: Full length-genome sequencing is achieved with Tiled-ClickSeq, including the 5'UTR which is missed in the bulk of current high-throughput sequencing efforts.
source: Full length-genome sequencing is achieved, including the 5'UTR which is missed in the bulk of current high-throughput sequencing efforts, removing the need for 5'RACE.
evidence: This is a key advantage of the method demonstrated in the study.

claim: Genome coverage began to drop concomitantly with the viral titer of the specimen, with samples with a CT value lower than 25 providing the best quality sequence data.
source: With only 18 PCR cycles, genome coverage began to drop concomitantly with the viral titer of the specimen, with samples with a CT value lower than 25 providing the best quality sequence data.
evidence: This is a finding about the relationship between viral load and sequencing quality.

claim: All the B.1.1.7 variants characterized from clinical samples contained a U2C SNV.
source: From these samples, we found that all the B.1.1.7 variants characterized contained a U2C SNV.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the analysis of clinical B.1.1.7 samples.

claim: The U2C SNV may be significant as the 5'UTR contains many important regulatory elements that impact replication and translation as well as recombination events.
source: In either case, this may be significant as the 5'UTR contains many important regulatory elements that impact replication and translation as well as recombination events that generate the viral sgmRNAs (Li et al., 2008; Zuniga et al., 2004) and therefore may impact viral fitness.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential significance of the U2C SNV, supported by citations about 5'UTR function.

claim: Small deletions such as the furin cleavage site 'PRRA' and the 'QTQTN' motif upstream of the site are prevalent among cell-passaged and amplified isolates of SARS-CoV-2.
source: Small deletions such as the actual furin cleave site 'PRRA' and the 'QTQTN' motif upstream of the site are prevalent among cell-passaged and amplified isolates of SARS-CoV-2 (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Deletions near the furin cleavage site confer a strong selection advantage in Vero E6 cells.
source: Indeed, we recently demonstrated that these deletions confer a strong selection advantage in Vero E6 cells, rationalizing their common occurrence in in vitro preparations (Johnson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Despite observing deletions near the furin cleavage site in almost all of the cell-culture isolates, no evidence of small deletions was found in 59 out of 60 clinical specimens analyzed.
source: It is surprising therefore that despite observing these deletions in almost all of the cell-culture isolates to some small degree, we did not find any evidence of small deletions in the 60 clinical specimens analyzed here with the exception of one sample (MicroGNL_163).
evidence: This is a comparative finding between cell-culture and clinical samples.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 may be poised to generate structural variants near the furin cleavage site, but they are not observed in primary human samples and thus not selected for during human infections.
source: This suggests that while SARS-CoV-2 may be poised to generate structural variants in this region, they are not observed in primary human samples and thus not selected for during human infections.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed difference between cell-culture and clinical samples.

claim: D-RNAs are a true component of the intrahost diversity of clinical specimens of SARS-CoV-2, albeit at low abundance and highly variable from sample to sample.
source: Recombination analysis using ViReMa confirms that D-RNAs are a true component of the intrahost diversity of clinical specimens of SARS-CoV-2, albeit at low abundance and are highly variable from sample to sample in terms of their precise junctions.
evidence: This is a finding from the recombination analysis of clinical samples.

claim: The 29442^29,323 recombination event is a 120nt duplication that maintains the open reading frame in the C-terminal end of Nucleocapsid (N) at residues 350–389.
source: The 29442^29,323 event is a 120nt duplication that maintains the open reading frame in the C-terminal end of Nucleocapsid (N) at residues 350–389, which contains the last 10 structured amino acids of the C-terminal domain (Peng et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a characterization of a specific recombination event, with structural information supported by a citation.

claim: The 29442^29,323 recombination event is not found in any of the cell-culture derived samples, suggesting it is purged during expansion and isolation.
source: Interestingly, this event is not found in any of the cell-culture derived samples suggesting that it is purged during expansion and isolation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed distribution of this recombination event.

claim: Genomic duplication followed by 'resolution' through a series of recombination events is a common mechanism observed in RNA viruses that allows for virus diversification and evolution.
source: Genomic duplication followed by 'resolution' through a series of recombination events is a common mechanism observed in RNA viruses that allows for virus diversification and evolution of the duplicated regions (Scheel et al., 2013; Bentley et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Large duplications may not be resolved when using paired-primer genomics approaches as these would generate amplicons larger than expected.
source: Such large duplications may not be resolved when using paired-primer genomics approaches as these would generate amplicons larger than expected and so may be filtered out during final NGS library size selection or during bioinformatic processing.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of paired-primer methods.

claim: The design of Tiled-ClickSeq imparts built-in quality control tools, including UMIs in the click-adaptor and the opportunity to use paired-end sequencing to identify the primer that gives rise to each amplicon.
source: The design of Tiled-ClickSeq imparts built-in quality control tools, including UMIs in the click-adaptor and the opportunity to use paired-end sequencing to identify the primer that gives rise to each amplicon.
evidence: This describes features of the method design.

claim: Information about primer efficiency can be used to determine the relative sensitivity and specificity of each primer in the primer mix, allowing the scheme to be pruned and optimized.
source: This information can be used to identify primers that yield poor viral priming efficiency and therefore a more specific primer can be designed and substituted as needed.
evidence: This is an inference about how the method can be optimized.

claim: The final primer scheme (v3) contained over 390 unique SARS-CoV-2 primers.
source: Our final primer scheme contained over 390 unique SARS-CoV-2 primers.
evidence: This is a specific detail about the method design.

claim: The Tiled-ClickSeq pipeline can accommodate complex mixtures of overlapping primers within the same RT reaction.
source: This purposely thorough design demonstrates how the Tiled-ClickSeq pipeline can accommodate complex mixtures of overlapping primers within the same RT reaction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the use of 390+ primers in the study.

claim: Built-in redundancy in the primer design reduces the chance of primer dropout due to the presence of SNVs, SVs or recombination events found in primer-annealing sites.
source: This built-in redundancy reduces the chance of primer dropout due to the presence of SNVs, SVs or recombination events found in primer-annealing sites.
evidence: This is an inference about an advantage of the method design.

claim: Very few minority variants were detected in the samples present above 2%.
source: Interestingly, we detected very few minority variants in our samples present above 2%.
evidence: This is a finding from the minority variant analysis.

claim: The low rate of minority variants is consistent with other reports of minority variant detection in SARS-CoV-2 isolates and likely reflects the activity of the coronavirus ExoN-nsp14 as a 'proof-reader' enzyme.
source: This is consistent with other reports of minority variant detection in SARS-CoV-2 isolates and likely reflects the well-characterized activity of the coronavirus ExoN-nsp14 as a 'proof-reader' enzyme (Smith and Denison, 2013).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation about the ExoN-nsp14 enzyme.

claim: The greatest source of genetic diversity in coronavirus isolates may be due to RNA recombination.
source: As a result, the greatest source of genetic diversity in coronavirus isolates may well be due to RNA recombination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low rate of SNVs and the abundance of recombination events observed.

claim: On the nanopore sequencing platform, sequence reads could be obtained within the same day as RNA extraction.
source: On the nanopore sequencing platform, we could obtain sequence reads within the same day as RNA extraction.
evidence: This describes the speed of the nanopore platform.

claim: The baseline accuracy rate of the nanopore platform prevents the reliable annotation of minority variants present at <5%.
source: While the baseline accuracy rate of the nanopore platform prevents the reliable annotation of minority variants present at <5%, this platform can reconstruct novel SARS-CoV-2 variants as well as identify abundant sgmRNAs.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the nanopore platform.

claim: The nanopore platform can reconstruct novel SARS-CoV-2 variants as well as identify abundant sgmRNAs.
source: While the baseline accuracy rate of the nanopore platform prevents the reliable annotation of minority variants present at <5%, this platform can reconstruct novel SARS-CoV-2 variants as well as identify abundant sgmRNAs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the study.

claim: Nanopore sequencing allows for identification of long-range epistatically linked variants.
source: Nanopore sequencing also allows for identification of long-range epistatically linked variants (Gallardo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The ARTIC protocol contains a primer cognate to the 5'UTR of SARS-CoV-2 (nts 30–54) to capture and quantitate sub-genomic mRNAs.
source: The ARTIC protocol contains a primer cognate to the 5'UTR of SARS-CoV-2 (nts 30–54) to capture and quantitate sub-genomic mRNAs (Parker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing the ARTIC protocol.

claim: Recombination events including non-canonical sgmRNAs will be missed by primer-pools that do not happen to flank RNA recombination junctions.
source: However, recombination events including non-canonical sgmRNAs will be missed by primer-pools that do not happen to flank RNA recombination junctions.
evidence: This is an inference about a limitation of paired-primer methods.

claim: Tiled-ClickSeq is capable of 'agnostically' detecting any unanticipated RNA recombination including D-RNAs.
source: In contrast, Tiled-ClickSeq is capable of 'agnostically' detecting any unanticipated RNA recombination including D-RNAs that can be characterized by RNA recombination events in or between any region of the viral genome, often in an unpredictable manner.
evidence: This is a claim about the capability of the method supported by the data.

claim: ClickSeq was originally designed to avoid artefactual recombination with fewer than three artefactual chimeric reads found per million reads.
source: As ClickSeq was originally designed to avoid artefactual recombination with fewer than three artefactual chimeric reads found per million reads, Tiled-ClickSeq provides a useful tool to identify D-RNAs and to robustly characterize rates of RNA recombination.
evidence: This is supported by the original design and validation of ClickSeq.
